name_en: Liu An Lan Cha (Anhui Basket Tea)
cultivar: Qimen small-leaf population bushes (the same stock as Keemun)
processing: Post-fermented basket tea: late-spring leaf is pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, left out to take the night dew so a slow fermentation starts, then steamed, packed into small bamboo baskets lined with bamboo leaves, fired gently in stacks of baskets and stored to mature.
harvest_season: Late spring, around Guyu, from leaf picked after the Keemun black-tea harvest; the tea is then made and basketed in early summer.
appearance_dry: Lightly matted dark-brown leaf in a small bamboo basket of about 500 g, lined and topped with dried bamboo leaves.
appearance_liquor: Amber to orange-red, clear, darkening with age.
appearance_wet: Small, even dark-brown leaves, tender for a dark tea.
taste_profile: Mild, sweet and smooth with bamboo leaf, a light betel-nut woodiness and a faint herbal, medicinal note; aged baskets gain depth and a cooling finish.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, boiling water, short steeps; drop a piece of the bamboo-leaf lining into the pot, as the Guangdong tea houses do. Young baskets are better simmered briefly.

vintage_note: Sold by the year the basket was made, usually as whole 500 g baskets and sometimes repacked loose; market lots run from the current year to 20+ years, with young baskets (1–3 years) a little green and astringent and 5–15 years the usual drinking range. Baskets from the 1980s–90s revival under the Sun Yi Shun name are collectables.
description:
Liu An Lan Cha is Anhui's one dark tea, and it is a tea with a geography problem: it is named after Lu'an, the city that once traded it, but it is made in Qimen County, the home of Keemun, from the same small-leaf bushes. For a century or more it was a Cantonese and Southeast Asian tea, carried south in small bamboo baskets and sold in Hong Kong and Malaysia alongside Liu Bao, often by herbalists who regarded it as cooling and good for the stomach. The old Sun Yi Shun brand is the name that survives from that trade; production stopped in the mid-twentieth century and was revived in the 1980s.

It is made quite differently from the Hunan and Guangxi teas. Late-spring leaf is pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, then left out to take the night dew, which starts a slow, mild fermentation; it is steamed, packed into small bamboo baskets lined with bamboo leaves, fired gently in stacks and put away to mature. There is no big pile and no smoke, which is why it stays light and clean, closer in spirit to a gently aged tea than to a brick.

In the cup it is mild, sweet and smooth with bamboo leaf, a light betel-nut woodiness and a faint herbal note; aged baskets deepen and pick up a cooling, medicinal finish without losing their gentleness. Brew it with boiling water after a rinse and it gives eight or nine steeps; a piece of the bamboo-leaf lining in the pot is traditional and adds to the flavour. Young baskets can be a touch green and astringent and are better after a few years or simmered briefly.

It is sold by basket year, mostly in 500 g baskets, by a few Qimen makers and through Hong Kong and Guangdong dealers; the Sun Yi Shun name is the historic one and the one most imitated. Look for an intact basket with a clean, sweet, bamboo smell; the tea should be dry and springy, not damp. Old baskets command high prices on the strength of the name, and the cup, not the label, is the only check on them.

If you like Liu Bao but want something lighter and more delicate, this is the tea; if you drink Keemun, it is the strange other life of the same bushes.
sources_note: The night-dew ('ye lu') step and the gentle basket firing follow Chinese descriptions of the traditional method; the 1980s revival and the Sun Yi Shun brand history are from trade accounts. 'Lu'an' is the standard reading of 六安, though 'Liu An' is common in tea-shop usage.
